screens.title: Introduction to AWS Network Monitoring Tools
screens.narratorSegment: In dynamic cloud networks you need tools that tell you what is happening, who changed things, and whether traffic is reaching its destination. In this lesson we introduce three AWS services that together provide that visibility: Amazon CloudWatch, which collects metrics and raises alarms; VPC Flow Logs, which record IP-level traffic flows; and AWS CloudTrail, which captures A P I activity for auditing and troubleshooting. You will learn not only what each service reports, but how they complement one another during incident response and performance tuning. For example, CloudWatch helps you spot a spike in bytes out, VPC Flow Logs show which IP pairs were active, and CloudTrail shows whether a security group rule was recently changed. We will also cover practical steps: creating an SNS topic for alerts, building a CloudWatch dashboard for NetworkIn and NetworkOut, and using metric alarms to avoid surprise outages. By the end of this chapter you will understand which tool to consult first for common network problems, how to configure a basic alarm, and how to avoid common mistakes like alert fatigue or missing the right metric resolution. Keep an eye out for a terminal-style CLI walkthrough and a hands-on dashboard activity that reinforce these ideas.

screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will identify the core AWS network monitoring services, understand their distinct roles, and configure a basic alarm and dashboard. First, you will be able to name Amazon CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, and AWS CloudTrail as the primary tools and explain what each records. Second, you will differentiate when to consult metrics, when to inspect flow records, and when to review A P I audit trails during troubleshooting. These skills matter because a single view rarely answers all operational questions: a metric spike needs flow evidence to confirm traffic patterns and audit logs to check for configuration changes. You will also practice configuring CloudWatch metrics and setting an alarm that notifies through an SNS topic, reinforcing how to turn visibility into action. Finally, you will learn why proactive monitoring and sensible thresholds prevent noisy alerts and how to choose the right metric granularity for your use case. Each objective is framed so you can demonstrate competency: name, differentiate, configure, and reason about monitoring choices.

screens.title: Why proactive network monitoring matters
screens.narratorSegment: Proactive monitoring means collecting and acting on signals before an incident becomes an outage. In an AWS environment, components scale and change frequently, so reactive troubleshooting alone is costly and slow. Start by defining what problem you want to prevent — for example, sustained network egress saturation, intermittent connectivity to an upstream A P I, or unauthorized configuration changes. Each of these requires different evidence: performance counters for saturation, flow records for connectivity paths, and audit logs for configuration changes. A clear monitoring strategy aligns metrics, flow logs, and audit trails to those questions. For instance, if you want to prevent bandwidth saturation, you capture NetworkIn and NetworkOut metrics in CloudWatch, set an alarm that triggers early, and create a dashboard to track trends. If you worry about lateral movement or unexpected connections, enable VPC Flow Logs to see source and destination IP pairs, and retain those logs for forensic queries. Finally, if you are concerned about configuration drift, use CloudTrail to record A P I activity and link alarms to A P I events when appropriate. A common misconception is that more data equals better monitoring; in practice, meaningful thresholds and alert routing determine whether monitoring helps or creates noise. Think about who receives an alert, how it escalates, and what playbook matches the alert. This mindset turns data into actionable operational behavior.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Why proactive monitoring matters
Definition

Proactive monitoring for AWS networks

Collect metrics, logs, and audit trails aligned to your critical network questions. Metrics show volume and health, flow logs show connectivity, and CloudTrail shows who changed configurations.

Example scenario
You see rising NetworkOut on an EC2 instance. CloudWatch identifies the spike; VPC Flow Logs show which remote IPs received traffic; CloudTrail reveals a recent deployment that changed outbound behavior.
Common misconception
More logs alone won't help if you don't set meaningful alarms or map logs to actions. Focus on signal, not volume.
Checklist
  • Define the critical network metric or event you care about.
  • Choose CloudWatch metrics for volume, VPC Flow Logs for connection details, CloudTrail for changes.
  • Create an alarm with a clear action and owner to avoid alert fatigue.
Key Takeaway

Monitoring works when signals map to actions. Use metrics, flows, and audit logs together and design alerts that your team can act on.

screens.title: Amazon CloudWatch — metrics, logs, and alarms
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon CloudWatch is the primary telemetry hub for AWS resources. It collects metrics that are time-ordered numeric data points such as NetworkIn and NetworkOut for EC2 instances, and aggregated counts like HealthyHostCount for load balancers. CloudWatch also ingests log files from services and custom applications. The main value of CloudWatch in a networking context is twofold: visibility and automation. Visibility means you can track throughput, packet rates and error conditions over time. Automation comes from alarms: you can define thresholds on a metric or math expression and trigger actions like sending a message to an SNS topic, invoking a Lambda, or auto-scaling. When configuring a metric alarm, choose an appropriate statistic and period — for example summing NetworkOut over a five-minute window to detect sustained high egress. A common beginner error is setting thresholds that are too tight or too loose; tune thresholds against a known baseline to reduce false positives. Dashboards let you combine multiple widgets so you can correlate NetworkIn/NetworkOut with C P U utilization or other signals. Use dashboards during incident response to get context quickly. In short, CloudWatch gives you numerical and temporal context and the ability to turn those signals into automated notifications and remediation steps.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › CloudWatch — metrics & alarms
Core Concept

Metrics, logs, and alarms

CloudWatch collects time-series metrics and logs and uses alarms to notify or trigger automated actions. In networking, metrics such as NetworkIn and NetworkOut reveal throughput and trends.

Metric example
NetworkOut for an EC2 instance measured per minute, summed over five minutes to detect sustained egress.
Alarm action
When a metric crosses a threshold, notify an SNS topic or invoke a Lambda to automate a response.
Supporting notes
  • Choose period and statistic that match the problem: use Sum over 5 minutes for bandwidth bursts.
  • Attach alarm-actions to an SNS topic to route notifications to email, chat, or automation.
  • Tune thresholds based on baseline to avoid alert fatigue.
Concrete example
Create an alarm when NetworkOut summed over five minutes exceeds 52,428,800 bytes (50 MB). Configure the alarm to notify an SNS topic subscribed by your operations inbox.

screens.title: Creating a CloudWatch alarm and SNS topic
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a CloudWatch alarm involves a small sequence of decisions and actions: choose the metric and dimensions, select an appropriate statistic and period, define the threshold and evaluation periods, and attach an alarm action. First, create an SNS topic to receive notifications and add subscribers such as an email address or Lambda. Then, pick the metric — for EC2 network egress choose NetworkOut and select the instance ID as a dimension. Use a five-minute period and Sum statistic for sustained bandwidth detection. Set the threshold at a value that reflects an abnormal sustained state rather than a short spike. Next, create the alarm and attach the SNS TopicArn as the alarm action. The chapter includes a CLI example; visually, think of the SNS topic as the delivery channel and the alarm as the watcher that pushes messages when conditions are met. A typical mistake is attaching too many recipients directly to the alarm; instead route through an SNS topic so you can manage subscriptions centrally. After creation, test the alarm by generating outbound traffic and confirm a notification is received. This process turns passive metrics into active operational signals that your team can act on.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Create an SNS topic, choose the right metric and window, set a meaningful threshold, and attach the SNS ARN as the alarm action to enable notifications.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Create alarm & SNS
Step-by-step
  1. Create an SNS topic and add a subscription for notifications.
  2. Choose the CloudWatch metric (NetworkOut) and select instance dimension.
  3. Pick statistic and period (Sum, 5 minutes) and set threshold.
  4. Attach alarm-actions to the SNS topic and name the alarm.
  5. Test by generating outbound traffic and verify notification arrives.
CLI example (visual only)
# Create SNS topic
aws sns create-topic --name NetworkPerformanceAlerts

# Use the TopicArn in a put-metric-alarm call
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "HighNetworkOutAlarm" \
  --alarm-description "Alarm when EC2 NetworkOut exceeds 50 MB/second for 5 minutes" \
  --metric-name NetworkOut \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Sum \
  --period 300 \
  --threshold 52428800 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abcdef1234567890 \
  --evaluation-periods 1 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:NetworkPerformanceAlerts \
  --unit Bytes
The code block shows the required parameters. Replace the instance ID and TopicArn for your environment.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs — who talks to whom
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs capture IP-level records about traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC. Each record includes source and destination IP addresses and ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether the packet was accepted or rejected. This granularity allows you to answer questions like: did traffic reach the instance, which remote IPs were communicating, and was traffic denied by security groups or network ACLs? Flow logs are invaluable when you need to confirm whether a connection attempt reached an interface or was blocked before reaching it. For security investigations, they show lateral movement patterns and unusual peers. For compliance and auditing, publishing flow logs to S3 preserves an immutable archive. For near real-time alerting, stream the logs to CloudWatch Logs and create metric filters that detect suspicious patterns. A common misunderstanding is treating flow logs as full packet captures — they are summaries of flows, not payloads. Use them alongside packet capture tools when you need deep packet inspection. Finally, consider retention and storage: storing all flow logs at high resolution can be costly, so plan retention and sampling according to your forensic requirements.

keyIdea.text: VPC Flow Logs record connection-level details to show which IP pairs communicated and whether traffic was accepted or rejected.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › VPC Flow Logs
What is recorded

IP-level flow records

Flow logs include source and destination IP, ports, protocol, bytes, packets, start and end times, and ACCEPT or REJECT action. They let you answer connectivity and security questions during investigation.

Use case: Connectivity troubleshooting
Confirm whether traffic reached the network interface or was denied earlier by a security group.
Use case: Security analysis
Identify unusual remote peers or lateral movement patterns by inspecting source-destination pairs over time.
Storage options
Publish flow logs to CloudWatch Logs for metric filters and real-time alerting, or to S3 for long-term archival and compliance. Many teams use both: CloudWatch for live ops and S3 for forensics.
Limitations
Flow logs summarize flows and do not capture packet payloads. For deep packet inspection, use packet capture tools in addition to flow logs.

screens.title: Choosing where to send flow logs
screens.narratorSegment: When enabling VPC Flow Logs you must decide where to publish them. CloudWatch Logs enables near real-time analysis: you can create metric filters and alarms that detect suspicious connection attempts or volume anomalies almost immediately. That makes CloudWatch Logs ideal for operations teams who need fast detection and automated responses. Publishing to S3 is a better choice when you require long-term archival, cost-effective storage, or batch forensic analysis. S3 archives are easier to query with batch tools and support immutable retention policies for compliance. Many architectures use both: stream raw flow logs to S3 for archival and simultaneously publish to CloudWatch Logs for live monitoring. Consider cost and retention: high-volume VPCs can generate large amounts of flow data, so decide sampling, aggregation, or selective capture based on your forensic needs. Also plan how you will index and search logs; CloudWatch Logs supports queries but can become costly at scale. A common mistake is to enable full-resolution logs for every interface without a retention plan — that increases cost and noise. Instead, prioritize critical subnets or interfaces and use filters or aggregated sampling to control volume while retaining the investigative value you need.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Flow Logs: destination choices
Option A

CloudWatch Logs

Use CloudWatch Logs when you need quick analysis and alerts. Metric filters can detect suspicious patterns and drive CloudWatch Alarms.

- Near real-time alerting
- Built-in query and metric filters
- Higher cost for large volumes
Option B

Amazon S3

Publish flow logs to S3 for archival storage and batch forensics. Use lifecycle policies for retention and cost control.

- Cost-effective long-term storage
- Good for compliance and batch analysis
- Requires external tooling for near real-time alerts
Recommended pattern
Stream to both CloudWatch Logs for operational alerts and to S3 for archival. Filter and sample where appropriate to manage costs and focus on critical traffic sources.

screens.title: AWS CloudTrail — auditing API activity
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CloudTrail records A P I activity across your AWS account, capturing who made changes, which A P I calls were used, and when they occurred. In a networking context this is essential for tracing configuration changes such as security group modifications, route table updates, or VPC peering events. When a connectivity regression or security exposure appears, CloudTrail helps you identify whether a recent change caused it and who initiated that change. Each CloudTrail event contains metadata like the caller identity, source IP, request parameters, and response. Use CloudTrail events to build alerts when specific APIs run, for example when a security group ingress rule is added that opens SSH from anywhere. A common misuse is treating CloudTrail as a metrics source; it is an audit trail for governance, not a performance metric stream. For effective investigations, centralize CloudTrail logs across accounts and regions into a single S3 bucket and consider streaming them into CloudWatch Logs to create metric filters for A P I-driven alerts. Together with CloudWatch and VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail completes the trio: metrics show the symptom, flow logs show the network-level evidence, and CloudTrail shows the configuration actions that could be the root cause.

keyIdea.title: CloudTrail role
keyIdea.text: CloudTrail provides an immutable audit trail of API activity, enabling you to trace configuration changes affecting network behavior.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › CloudTrail — audit logs
What CloudTrail records
  • API calls from console, CLI, or SDKs.
  • Who made the call, when, and from which IP.
  • Request parameters and responses that show what changed.
Network examples
- Security group rule changes like adding 0.0.0.0/0 to port 22.
- Route table modifications and VPC peering creation.
- Changes to VPN or Direct Connect configuration.
Best practice
Centralize CloudTrail logs and consider streaming to CloudWatch Logs to create metric filters for API-change detection and automated response playbooks.

screens.title: How CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, and CloudTrail work together
screens.narratorSegment: When troubleshooting network issues, reach for the right tool in sequence. Start with CloudWatch to identify if there is an observable performance change: are NetworkIn or NetworkOut spiking or dropping? CloudWatch gives you the numeric symptom and timing. Next, consult VPC Flow Logs to verify whether the packets flowed between expected IP pairs and whether they were accepted or rejected. Flow logs provide the who and where in the network plane. Finally, check CloudTrail to see whether a configuration change could explain the symptom — for example a security group rule removal or a route update. This layered approach reduces guesswork: CloudWatch reveals the symptom, Flow Logs provide the evidence, and CloudTrail provides the change history. A concrete example: a sudden drop in HealthyHostCount on a load balancer appears in CloudWatch. Flow logs show backend instances stopped accepting connections from the load balancer's health port. CloudTrail may reveal a recent deployment that changed a security group or instance configuration. A common error is using only one of these services to make a root-cause claim; instead correlate across them and you’ll arrive at confident conclusions faster.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › CLI demo
What to capture
  • Topic name and ARN for SNS.
  • Metric name, namespace, statistic, period.
  • Dimensions to scope the alarm to a specific instance.
  • Alarm-actions that reference the SNS TopicArn.
Visual CLI block
# Create SNS topic
aws sns create-topic --name NetworkPerformanceAlerts

# Create CloudWatch alarm for NetworkOut
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "HighNetworkOutAlarm" \
  --alarm-description "Alarm when EC2 NetworkOut exceeds 50 MB/second for 5 minutes" \
  --metric-name NetworkOut \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Sum \
  --period 300 \
  --threshold 52428800 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abcdef1234567890 \
  --evaluation-periods 1 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:NetworkPerformanceAlerts \
  --unit Bytes
This visual block is a template; replace instance ID and TopicArn when you run it.

screens.title: Build a CloudWatch dashboard for network metrics
screens.narratorSegment: A CloudWatch dashboard gives you a single pane of glass to correlate network and compute signals. Start by creating a new dashboard and add a line widget for NetworkIn and NetworkOut for your EC2 instance. Next add a CPUUtilization widget to provide context: if both C P U and network are high, the instance may be saturated; if only network is high, consider network capacity or instance type. screens.title: Troubleshoot EC2 network latency using all three tools
screens.narratorSegment: Imagine you notice increased network latency for an application on an EC2 instance. First, consult CloudWatch metrics: check NetworkIn and NetworkOut for spikes or drops and confirm C P U and HealthyHostCount to rule out compute or backend health issues. If CloudWatch shows a sudden drop in NetworkIn, open your VPC Flow Logs to determine whether the traffic from expected client IPs reached the instance and whether the action was ACCEPT or REJECT. Flow logs will show source and destination IPs and ports, helping you discover if traffic was blocked by a security group or NACL. If flow logs indicate traffic was rejected or unexpectedly absent, use CloudTrail to search for recent A P I calls that changed network configuration, such as AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, RevokeSecurityGroupIngress, or route table modifications. Correlate timestamps: the alarm time, flow log entries, and CloudTrail event time to build a timeline. A common pitfall is stopping after CloudWatch analysis; use flow logs to know whether packets arrived and CloudTrail to find configuration changes. This three-step correlation helps you produce a clear incident report: symptom, evidence, and change that likely caused it.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Troubleshooting Scenario
Guided steps
  1. Check CloudWatch for NetworkIn/NetworkOut, CPU, and HealthyHostCount.
  2. Inspect VPC Flow Logs for source-destination pairs and ACCEPT/REJECT actions.
  3. Search CloudTrail for recent security group, route table, or instance configuration changes.
  4. Correlate timestamps to build a timeline and identify the likely root cause.
  5. Create a remediation plan based on evidence and document the incident.
Scenario example
CloudWatch shows a drop in NetworkIn at 10:12. Flow logs show many rejects from the load balancer IP on port 80 at 10:12. CloudTrail shows a security group change at 10:11 that removed the healthcheck rule. Timeline created: change, rejects, symptom.
Common mistake
Declaring root cause from a single source. Always correlate metrics, flow logs, and CloudTrail events to avoid false conclusions.

Finally, choose storage and retention thoughtfully: CloudWatch and CloudWatch Logs for near real-time operation, S3 for long-term archival and compliance. These practical habits keep your network observable and your team effective during incident response.

fullNarratorScript:
In dynamic cloud networks you need tools that tell you what is happening, who changed things, and whether traffic is reaching its destination. In this lesson we introduce three AWS services that together provide that visibility: Amazon CloudWatch, which collects metrics and raises alarms; VPC Flow Logs, which record IP-level traffic flows; and AWS CloudTrail, which captures A P I activity for auditing and troubleshooting. You will learn not only what each service reports, but how they complement one another during incident response and performance tuning. For example, CloudWatch helps you spot a spike in bytes out, VPC Flow Logs show which IP pairs were active, and CloudTrail shows whether a security group rule was recently changed. We will also cover practical steps: creating an SNS topic for alerts, building a CloudWatch dashboard for NetworkIn and NetworkOut, and using metric alarms to avoid surprise outages. By the end of this chapter you will understand which tool to consult first for common network problems, how to configure a basic alarm, and how to avoid common mistakes like alert fatigue or missing the right metric resolution. Keep an eye out for a terminal-style CLI walkthrough and a hands-on dashboard activity that reinforce these ideas.

By the end of this chapter you will identify the core AWS network monitoring services, understand their distinct roles, and configure a basic alarm and dashboard. First, you will be able to name Amazon CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, and AWS CloudTrail as the primary tools and explain what each records. Second, you will differentiate when to consult metrics, when to inspect flow records, and when to review A P I audit trails during troubleshooting. These skills matter because a single view rarely answers all operational questions: a metric spike needs flow evidence to confirm traffic patterns and audit logs to check for configuration changes. You will also practice configuring CloudWatch metrics and setting an alarm that notifies through an SNS topic, reinforcing how to turn visibility into action. Finally, you will learn why proactive monitoring and sensible thresholds prevent noisy alerts and how to choose the right metric granularity for your use case. Each objective is framed so you can demonstrate competency: name, differentiate, configure, and reason about monitoring choices.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying monitoring to real scenarios and mastering operational judgment. You will learn to configure a dashboard that surfaces NetworkIn and NetworkOut alongside C P U utilization, providing context that helps distinguish network saturation from C P U-bound performance. Next, you will practice streaming VPC Flow Logs either to CloudWatch Logs for near real-time alerting and analysis, or to S3 for archival and compliance, and learn when each option is appropriate. You will also use CloudTrail to trace configuration changes that could cause connectivity issues, such as a modified security group or a new route. Importantly, you will be trained to avoid two common pitfalls: monitoring only at a too-coarse level which misses transient spikes, and creating alarm thresholds that cause alert fatigue. The goal is to combine data sources into actionable signals and to reason about who should be notified and how the alerts should escalate during an incident.

Proactive monitoring means collecting and acting on signals before an incident becomes an outage. In an AWS environment, components scale and change frequently, so reactive troubleshooting alone is costly and slow. Start by defining what problem you want to prevent — for example, sustained network egress saturation, intermittent connectivity to an upstream A P I, or unauthorized configuration changes. Each of these requires different evidence: performance counters for saturation, flow records for connectivity paths, and audit logs for configuration changes. A clear monitoring strategy aligns metrics, flow logs, and audit trails to those questions. For instance, if you want to prevent bandwidth saturation, you capture NetworkIn and NetworkOut metrics in CloudWatch, set an alarm that triggers early, and create a dashboard to track trends. If you worry about lateral movement or unexpected connections, enable VPC Flow Logs to see source and destination IP pairs, and retain those logs for forensic queries. Finally, if you are concerned about configuration drift, use CloudTrail to record A P I activity and link alarms to A P I events when appropriate. A common misconception is that more data equals better monitoring; in practice, meaningful thresholds and alert routing determine whether monitoring helps or creates noise. Think about who receives an alert, how it escalates, and what playbook matches the alert. This mindset turns data into actionable operational behavior.

Amazon CloudWatch is the primary telemetry hub for AWS resources. It collects metrics that are time-ordered numeric data points such as NetworkIn and NetworkOut for EC2 instances, and aggregated counts like HealthyHostCount for load balancers. CloudWatch also ingests log files from services and custom applications. The main value of CloudWatch in a networking context is twofold: visibility and automation. Visibility means you can track throughput, packet rates and error conditions over time. Automation comes from alarms: you can define thresholds on a metric or math expression and trigger actions like sending a message to an SNS topic, invoking a Lambda, or auto-scaling. When configuring a metric alarm, choose an appropriate statistic and period — for example summing NetworkOut over a five-minute window to detect sustained high egress. A common beginner error is setting thresholds that are too tight or too loose; tune thresholds against a known baseline to reduce false positives. Dashboards let you combine multiple widgets so you can correlate NetworkIn/NetworkOut with C P U utilization or other signals. Use dashboards during incident response to get context quickly. In short, CloudWatch gives you numerical and temporal context and the ability to turn those signals into automated notifications and remediation steps.

Setting up a CloudWatch alarm involves a small sequence of decisions and actions: choose the metric and dimensions, select an appropriate statistic and period, define the threshold and evaluation periods, and attach an alarm action. First, create an SNS topic to receive notifications and add subscribers such as an email address or Lambda. Then, pick the metric — for EC2 network egress choose NetworkOut and select the instance ID as a dimension. Use a five-minute period and Sum statistic for sustained bandwidth detection. Set the threshold at a value that reflects an abnormal sustained state rather than a short spike. Next, create the alarm and attach the SNS TopicArn as the alarm action. The chapter includes a CLI example; visually, think of the SNS topic as the delivery channel and the alarm as the watcher that pushes messages when conditions are met. A typical mistake is attaching too many recipients directly to the alarm; instead route through an SNS topic so you can manage subscriptions centrally. After creation, test the alarm by generating outbound traffic and confirm a notification is received. This process turns passive metrics into active operational signals that your team can act on.

VPC Flow Logs capture IP-level records about traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC. Each record includes source and destination IP addresses and ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether the packet was accepted or rejected. This granularity allows you to answer questions like: did traffic reach the instance, which remote IPs were communicating, and was traffic denied by security groups or network ACLs? Flow logs are invaluable when you need to confirm whether a connection attempt reached an interface or was blocked before reaching it. For security investigations, they show lateral movement patterns and unusual peers. For compliance and auditing, publishing flow logs to S3 preserves an immutable archive. For near real-time alerting, stream the logs to CloudWatch Logs and create metric filters that detect suspicious patterns. A common misunderstanding is treating flow logs as full packet captures — they are summaries of flows, not payloads. Use them alongside packet capture tools when you need deep packet inspection. Finally, consider retention and storage: storing all flow logs at high resolution can be costly, so plan retention and sampling according to your forensic requirements.

When enabling VPC Flow Logs you must decide where to publish them. CloudWatch Logs enables near real-time analysis: you can create metric filters and alarms that detect suspicious connection attempts or volume anomalies almost immediately. That makes CloudWatch Logs ideal for operations teams who need fast detection and automated responses. Publishing to S3 is a better choice when you require long-term archival, cost-effective storage, or batch forensic analysis. S3 archives are easier to query with batch tools and support immutable retention policies for compliance. Many architectures use both: stream raw flow logs to S3 for archival and simultaneously publish to CloudWatch Logs for live monitoring. Consider cost and retention: high-volume VPCs can generate large amounts of flow data, so decide sampling, aggregation, or selective capture based on your forensic needs. Also plan how you will index and search logs; CloudWatch Logs supports queries but can become costly at scale. A common mistake is to enable full-resolution logs for every interface without a retention plan — that increases cost and noise. Instead, prioritize critical subnets or interfaces and use filters or aggregated sampling to control volume while retaining the investigative value you need.

AWS CloudTrail records A P I activity across your AWS account, capturing who made changes, which A P I calls were used, and when they occurred. In a networking context this is essential for tracing configuration changes such as security group modifications, route table updates, or VPC peering events. When a connectivity regression or security exposure appears, CloudTrail helps you identify whether a recent change caused it and who initiated that change. Each CloudTrail event contains metadata like the caller identity, source IP, request parameters, and response. Use CloudTrail events to build alerts when specific APIs run, for example when a security group ingress rule is added that opens SSH from anywhere. A common misuse is treating CloudTrail as a metrics source; it is an audit trail for governance, not a performance metric stream. For effective investigations, centralize CloudTrail logs across accounts and regions into a single S3 bucket and consider streaming them into CloudWatch Logs to create metric filters for A P I-driven alerts. Together with CloudWatch and VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail completes the trio: metrics show the symptom, flow logs show the network-level evidence, and CloudTrail shows the configuration actions that could be the root cause.

When troubleshooting network issues, reach for the right tool in sequence. Start with CloudWatch to identify if there is an observable performance change: are NetworkIn or NetworkOut spiking or dropping? CloudWatch gives you the numeric symptom and timing. Next, consult VPC Flow Logs to verify whether the packets flowed between expected IP pairs and whether they were accepted or rejected. Flow logs provide the who and where in the network plane. Finally, check CloudTrail to see whether a configuration change could explain the symptom — for example a security group rule removal or a route update.
